dayalike: Whose Day Is It?

Which kind of day did you have, and what makes it that kind of day?

dayalike compares one day of your time use with eight types of day found in the diaries of 6,146 people in the 2025 American Time Use Survey. It is for anyone curious about how they spend their time. The package includes:

  • an interactive Shiny app, launched with run_app();
  • match_my_day(), which ranks the eight day types by how close they are to your day;
  • compare_day(), which shows which activities make your day similar to, or different from, a type;
  • the prepared survey data: atus_days, day_types, day_type_profiles and activity_categories.

Documentation website: https://etc5523-2026.github.io/etc5523-assignment-4-tzhu0035-png/

Installation 

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("ETC5523-2026/etc5523-assignment-4-tzhu0035-png")

Launch the app 

library(dayalike)
run_app()

Enter the hours you spent on each activity during one day, or start from an example day. The app shows the type your day looks most like, which activities explain the match, and how close every other type is.

Use the functions 

my_day <- c(sleep = 7.5, personal_care = 1, eating = 1, work = 9,
            housework = 1, screen = 2.5, travel = 1.5, exercise = 0.5)

match_my_day(my_day)
compare_day(my_day, "Work day")

See vignette("dayalike") for a full guide to the app and how to read its results.

Data

The data come from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, American Time Use Survey 2025, Activity Summary file (https://www.bls.gov/tus/data/datafiles-2025.htm). BLS data are in the public domain. The original file is kept in data-raw/atussum-2025.zip, and data-raw/atus_days.R turns it into the package data: it groups the detailed activities into 15 categories and groups the days into eight types with survey-weighted k-means clustering.
